intended_object: The set of consecutive (cyclically adjacent) ordered pairs (d, w) in a finite set D of directions in the plane: pairs of distinct members of D with no member of D strictly inside the counterclockwise arc from d to w. These pairs index the sectors that D cuts the circle (or a punctured disk) into. Inferred from the docstring, the module documentation and the definition of `IsSectorPair`.
explanation:
The body is `{p | IsSectorPair D p.1 p.2}`, which just repackages the predicate `IsSectorPair` as a set. That predicate says d ∈ D, w ∈ D, d ≠ w, and no v ∈ D lies in `arcCCW d w`. `arcCCW` is the open counterclockwise arc from d to w, defined by a cyclic sign condition on `det`, so it handles short arcs, long arcs and opposite directions alike. This is exactly the usual meaning of "d and w are consecutive in the cyclic order of D".

Degenerate cases also match what the module documents. With one direction, `arcCCW d d` is empty but d ≠ d fails, so there are no pairs. With two directions a and b, both (a, b) and (b, a) are pairs, giving the two complementary sectors.

The definition does not require D to be finite or to consist of unit vectors. Those hypotheses go into the lemmas instead (`sectorPairs_finite`, `exists_isSectorPair`). This is a harmless generalization, not an error.

The notion is specific to the cyclic order of directions in ℝ², so it is not too narrow. Mathlib has no counterpart for consecutive pairs of a finite set of plane directions.
